q: A compound with molecular formula C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>13</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> contains a benzene ring. What is its degree of unsaturation (DBE)?
h: DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H)/2. Oxygen does not change the count; each N adds one.
w: DBE = (2·10 + 2 + 1 − 13)/2 = 10/2 = 5. The benzene ring uses 4, so there is exactly one more ring or π bond (for example an amide or ester C=O).
x: 4 comes from subtracting the N instead of adding it: (22 − 1 − 13)/2. Nitrogen brings an extra H to a saturated formula, so it is added.
6 comes from treating each O like N; oxygen is divalent and does not change the H count of a saturated formula.
10 is the value of (2C + 2 + N − H) before dividing by 2; each degree of unsaturation removes two H, so the difference must be halved.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown. The δ 7.49 doublet and δ 6.72 dd share a 16 Hz coupling, and the δ 6.72 dd and δ 9.70 doublet share a 7.7 Hz coupling. Which structure fits?
h: DBE = 6. Which proton appears near δ 9.7 and why is it a doublet? What does J = 16 Hz say about a C=C?
w: DBE = (18 + 2 − 8)/2 = 6: a benzene ring plus two more (C=O and C=C). The δ 9.70 H with IR 2815/2740 cm−1 is an aldehyde H; it is a doublet because it is coupled to one vinyl H (δ 6.72). That vinyl H is also coupled (J = 16 Hz, trans) to the δ 7.49 H on the carbon bearing the phenyl group. The C=O at 1680 cm−1 is lowered by conjugation. The compound is (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enal (cinnamaldehyde).
x: 1-Phenylprop-2-yn-1-ol would show a broad O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a sharp ≡C–H near 3290 cm<sup>−1</sup>, no C=O band, and no signal near δ 9.7.
1-Indanone has four 1H aromatic signals, two 2H triplet-like CH<sub>2</sub> signals near δ 3.1 and 2.7, and no aldehyde H.
1-Phenylprop-2-en-1-one has a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> (two vinyl H near δ 5.9 and 6.4 plus a dd near δ 7.1) and no aldehyde H near δ 9.7.

q: Natural chlorine is 75.8% <sup>35</sup>Cl and 24.2% <sup>37</sup>Cl. What relative intensities are expected for the M, M+2 and M+4 peaks of 1,4-dichlorobenzene (ignore <sup>13</sup>C)?
h: Each Cl is independently 35 or 37. Multiply probabilities for the three combinations (35,35), (35,37 two ways), (37,37).
x: 100 : 32 is the pattern for one Cl (3 : 1). With two Cl atoms the chance that at least one is <sup>37</sup>Cl roughly doubles, and an M+4 peak appears.
The M+2 value is right, but a molecule with both Cl atoms as <sup>37</sup>Cl (0.242² ≈ 6%) gives a real M+4 peak.
100 : 196 : 96 (≈ 1 : 2 : 1) is the pattern for two Br atoms, whose isotopes are nearly 50 : 50.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: The 1 : 1 pair at the top of the spectrum tells you the halogen. The CH<sub>3</sub> splitting tells you its neighbor.
w: M+ at m/z 184/186 in a 1 : 1 ratio means one Br (C8H9Br). The base peak at m/z 105 is M − Br, a stabilized secondary benzylic cation. In the NMR, the 3H doublet (δ 2.04) and 1H quartet (δ 5.21) form a CH–CH3 unit; the CH is far downfield because it carries both Br and Ph. With a 5H ring, the compound is (1-bromoethyl)benzene.
x: (2-Bromoethyl)benzene has –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br: two 2H triplets near δ 3.55 and 3.15, no 3H doublet.
1-Bromo-4-ethylbenzene has the Br on the ring: two 2H doublets (4 ArH) and an ethyl quartet near δ 2.6 and triplet near δ 1.2.
(1-Chloroethyl)benzene would give M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 140/142 in a 3 : 1 ratio.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>11</sub>N shows one medium IR band at 3410 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the δ 3.55 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: One N–H band means a secondary amine. Then decide whether the CH<sub>2</sub> quartet at δ 3.13 is on N or on the ring, and look at the aromatic shifts.
w: One N–H stretch and a 1H exchangeable signal mean a secondary amine (N–H). The aromatic H are 5H in a 2:1:2 pattern with the ortho (δ 6.61) and para (δ 6.70) H shifted upfield by the electron-donating NH group, so N is on the ring. The ethyl CH2 quartet at δ 3.13 is on N (an Ar–CH2 would be near δ 2.6). The compound is N-ethylaniline.
x: 4-Ethylaniline is a primary amine (two N–H bands, 2H NH<sub>2</sub>), para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets), with its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 2.55.
N,N-Dimethylaniline has no N–H at all and shows a 6H singlet near δ 2.9.
N-Methylbenzylamine has an ordinary 5H phenyl multiplet near δ 7.3 (N is not on the ring) and two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.75, CH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.45).

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>3</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1725 and 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Assign the two carbonyl carbons (δ 197.6 and 166.3) to carbonyl types. Then decide where each CH<sub>3</sub> is attached from its 1H and 13C shifts.
w: DBE = 6: ring + two C=O. δ 197.6 is a conjugated ketone (1685 cm−1) and δ 166.3 a conjugated ester (1725 cm−1). The 3H singlet at δ 3.95 with 13C δ 52.4 is an ester O–CH3; the 3H singlet at δ 2.64 with 13C δ 26.9 is CH3C=O. Both aromatic doublets are far downfield (δ 8.11, 8.01) because both substituents withdraw electrons, and two 2H doublets mean para. The compound is methyl 4-acetylbenzoate.
x: 4-Acetylphenyl acetate has an aryl ester: C=O near 1765 cm<sup>−1</sup>, ester 13C near 169, an OC(=O)CH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 2.3 (13C ≈ 21) and no OCH<sub>3</sub> near δ 3.9; the ArH ortho to O would be near δ 7.2.
Methyl 3-acetylbenzoate is meta-substituted: four different aromatic H and 10 carbon signals, not two 2H doublets and 8 signals.
Methyl 2-(4-formylphenyl)acetate has an aldehyde (1H singlet near δ 10.0, 13C near 192) and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.7; its ester C=O (≈ 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, δ ≈ 171) is unconjugated.

q: At room temperature the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of N,N-dimethylacetamide shows three 3H singlets: δ 3.02, 2.94 and 2.09. Why do the two N–CH<sub>3</sub> groups give separate signals?
c: The C–N bond has partial double-bond character, so rotation is slow on the NMR time scale; one CH<sub>3</sub> is cis to O, the other trans
The nitrogen is a stereocenter that inverts slowly, which makes the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups diastereotopic
The two N–CH<sub>3</sub> groups split each other, so the pair at δ 3.02 and 2.94 is really one doublet
Rotation about the bond between C=O and the acetyl CH<sub>3</sub> is slow, which holds one N–CH<sub>3</sub> closer to that CH<sub>3</sub> group
h: Draw the resonance form of an amide that puts a double bond between C and N.
w: Amide resonance (O=C–NR2 ↔ −O–C=N+R2) gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character and a rotation barrier of roughly 75–85 kJ/mol. At room temperature the two N–CH3 groups do not exchange places quickly, so the one cis to O and the one trans to O are in different environments: slow C–N rotation. On heating, the two signals broaden and merge.
x: The amide N is planar (sp<sup>2</sup>, lone pair delocalized) and carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not a stereocenter.
Equivalent or not, CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the same N are four bonds apart and do not show resolved coupling; a doublet would also be one 6H signal, not two 3H singlets.
Rotation of a CH<sub>3</sub> about a C–C single bond is fast, and it cannot make the two N–CH<sub>3</sub> groups different.

q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>BrO<sub>2</sub> shows a very broad IR band from 3300 to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a strong band at 1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum (DMSO-d<sub>6</sub>) is shown; the δ 8.05 signal shows only small (≈ 1.8 Hz) couplings, and the δ 7.47 triplet has J ≈ 8 Hz. Which structure fits?
h: Four different 1H aromatic signals rule out para. Which ring H has no ortho neighbor at all?
w: The broad O–H, the exchangeable δ 13.3 H and C=O at 1690 cm−1 mean an aryl carboxylic acid. Four different aromatic H mean the ring is not para. The δ 8.05 H has only meta couplings, so it has no H on either adjacent carbon: it sits between the two substituents (C2 of a 1,3-disubstituted ring). The 1H triplet with J ≈ 8 Hz is H5, which has two ortho neighbors. That is the meta pattern: 3-bromobenzoic acid.
x: 4-Bromobenzoic acid is para-substituted: two 2H doublets, not four 1H signals.
In 2-bromobenzoic acid every ring H has at least one ortho neighbor, so every signal shows a large (≈ 8 Hz) coupling; none has only small couplings.
5-Bromo-2-hydroxybenzaldehyde has an aldehyde H singlet near δ 9.9 and a phenol O–H near δ 11, and only 3 aromatic H; it is not a carboxylic acid.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 4.05 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H bands and a 2H exchangeable signal: what kind of nitrogen? The ethyl quartet at δ 4.32 tells you which atom the CH<sub>2</sub> is on.
w: Two N–H stretches (3420, 3340 cm−1) and a 2H exchangeable signal mean an aryl NH2. The C=O at 1680 cm−1 is an ester lowered by conjugation with a ring carrying a strong donor. The CH2 quartet at δ 4.32 is on the ester O (O–CH2CH3). Two 2H doublets, one far upfield at δ 6.64 (ortho to NH2) and one at δ 7.86 (ortho to C=O), mean para. The compound is ethyl 4-aminobenzoate (benzocaine).
x: 4-Aminophenyl propanoate is an aryl ester: C=O near 1750 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the ethyl CH<sub>2</sub> quartet on the acyl side near δ 2.55; no aromatic H would be as far downfield as δ 7.86.
Ethyl 2-aminobenzoate is ortho-substituted: four different 1H aromatic signals, not two 2H doublets.
4-(Ethylamino)benzoic acid has one N–H (one band), a broad carboxylic O–H, an N–CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 3.2, and its exchangeable H are 1H (NH) plus 1H (COOH).

q: Which spectral change best confirms that the reaction shown gave the expected product?
c: The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, a strong band appears near 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 3H singlet appears near δ 2.57
The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, a strong band appears near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 3H singlet appears near δ 2.15
The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, a broad band appears near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 6H singlet appears near δ 1.55
The sharp 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears, two N–H bands appear near 3300–3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and a new 2H singlet appears near δ 3.8
h: A Grignard reagent adds once to a nitrile; the imine salt is hydrolyzed in step 2. What functional group results, and is it conjugated?
w: CH3MgBr adds once to C≡N to give an imine anion, which cannot add a second Grignard; aqueous acid hydrolyzes the imine to a ketone, 4-methylacetophenone. The C≡N band disappears and a ketone C=O appears near 1685 cm−1 (conjugated with the ring); the new CH3C=O singlet is near δ 2.57. So: 2228 cm−1 gone, C=O near 1685 cm−1, new 3H singlet near δ 2.57.
x: 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and δ 2.15 describe an unconjugated methyl ketone; here the C=O is attached directly to the ring, which lowers the stretch to about 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup> and moves the CH<sub>3</sub> to about δ 2.6.
A 3° alcohol with two new CH<sub>3</sub> groups would need two Grignard additions; the negatively charged imine intermediate does not react a second time.
A primary amine (ArCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) comes from reducing a nitrile with LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, not from a Grignard reagent.

q: Benzaldehyde and acetone react as shown (Claisen–Schmidt condensation). Which data best confirm that the product is (E)-4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one?
c: Two 1H doublets at δ 7.50 and 6.71 with J ≈ 16 Hz, a 3H singlet at δ 2.38, and a C=O band near 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup>
Two 1H doublets at δ 6.90 and 6.20 with J ≈ 11 Hz, a 3H singlet at δ 2.20, and a C=O band near 1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>
A 1H doublet at δ 9.70, a 1H dd at δ 6.72, a 1H doublet at δ 7.49, and a C=O band near 1680 cm<sup>−1</sup>
A 1H dd at δ 5.15, a 2H doublet at δ 2.85, a 3H singlet at δ 2.20, and bands near 3400 and 1712 cm<sup>−1</sup>
h: Condensation (with heat) means dehydration to a C=C conjugated with the C=O. What J value goes with a trans C=C?
w: Heating drives the aldol addition product to dehydrate, giving the conjugated enone PhCH=CHC(=O)CH3. Its two vinyl H are mutually coupled doublets; J ≈ 16 Hz shows they are trans (E). The β H (δ 7.50) is downfield of the α H (δ 6.71) because conjugation puts δ+ on the β carbon. The methyl ketone singlet is at δ 2.38 and the conjugated C=O is near 1670 cm−1. The answer is two doublets with J ≈ 16 Hz, a 3H singlet, C=O near 1670 cm−1.
x: J ≈ 11 Hz is a cis (Z) vinyl coupling; trans coupling is 12–18 Hz, typically about 16 Hz.
A δ 9.70 doublet is an aldehyde H; this describes cinnamaldehyde, not a methyl ketone.
A CH–O dd at δ 5.15, a CH2 doublet, an O–H band and an unconjugated C=O describe the aldol addition product (4-hydroxy-4-phenylbutan-2-one), which has not yet lost water.

q: Acetophenone is treated with mCPBA. The product (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) shows a strong IR band at 1765 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a strong band at 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is the product?
h: In a Baeyer–Villiger oxidation the group with higher migratory aptitude ends up on oxygen. Then check: is the CH<sub>3</sub> on O or on C=O?
w: Phenyl migrates in preference to methyl, so O is inserted between the ring and the C=O, giving phenyl acetate. The data agree: 1765 cm−1 is the high C=O stretch of an aryl ester (the O lone pair is shared with the ring, so it donates less to C=O), and the 3H singlet at δ 2.30 is CH3C=O, not O–CH3. The ring H ortho to O (δ 7.08) are upfield of ordinary benzene H. The product is phenyl acetate.
x: Methyl benzoate (from methyl migration) would show an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.9, ortho ArH near δ 8.0, and a conjugated ester C=O near 1725 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Phenylacetic acid shows a broad O–H (3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a δ 11–12 COOH, and a CH<sub>2</sub> singlet near δ 3.6; it is not a Baeyer–Villiger product.
4-Hydroxyacetophenone shows a phenol O–H, a conjugated ketone C=O near 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and two 2H doublets; mCPBA does not hydroxylate the ring.

q: Aniline has a UV absorption band at 280 nm. In dilute aqueous HCl this band disappears and the spectrum looks almost like benzene's (λ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 254 nm). What explains the shift?
c: Protonation ties up the N lone pair, so it no longer conjugates with the ring; the chromophore becomes benzene-like and λ<sub>max</sub> gets shorter
Protonation puts a positive charge in conjugation with the ring, which extends the π system and shrinks the HOMO–LUMO gap
Aqueous acid removes the NH<sub>2</sub> group from the ring, so the solution actually contains benzene and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
The new N–H bonds of the anilinium ion absorb strongly near 254 nm and hide the 280 nm band beneath them
h: Which electrons on aniline are part of the conjugated π system, and what happens to them on protonation?
w: In aniline the N lone pair is delocalized into the ring, raising the HOMO and shifting λmax to longer wavelength (280 nm). In the anilinium ion, C6H5NH3+, that pair forms an N–H σ bond and is no longer conjugated, so the chromophore is just the benzene ring: loss of lone-pair conjugation gives a shift to shorter wavelength (a hypsochromic or blue shift). Adding base reverses it.
x: A larger conjugated system would shift λmax to longer wavelength, the opposite of what is observed. The NH3+ group has no π electrons or p orbital to conjugate.
Dilute HCl only protonates the amine (an acid–base reaction); adding base restores the 280 nm band, which would be impossible if the C–N bond had broken.
N–H σ bonds absorb only in the far UV (below 200 nm); they do not produce a 254 nm band. That band is the benzene ring's own π → π* absorption.

q: Rank compounds I–III by λmax in the UV, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Only C=C bonds in one continuous conjugated system count. A CH<sub>2</sub> between two C=C breaks the conjugation.
w: In 1,4-pentadiene (I) the C=C bonds are separated by CH2, so they absorb like isolated alkenes (below 200 nm). 1,3-Butadiene (II) is a conjugated diene (≈ 217 nm), and 1,3,5-hexatriene (III) has three conjugated C=C (≈ 258 nm). More conjugation means a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap and longer λmax: I < II < III.
x: Having more carbons does not lengthen λ<sub>max</sub>; I has five carbons but no conjugation, so it absorbs at the shortest wavelength.
This is the reverse order; the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks, not grows, as conjugation increases.
I has isolated C=C bonds and absorbs at the shortest wavelength, not the longest.

q: A compound C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows a broad IR band at 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the δ 4.70 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: The broad band and exchangeable H mean O–H. Then count aromatic H and look at the pattern.
w: The broad 3300 cm−1 band and the exchangeable 1H at δ 4.70 mean an O–H. Only 4 aromatic H as two 2H doublets means para substitution, and the 3H singlet at δ 2.27 is an aryl CH3. The compound is 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).
x: Anisole has no O–H, a 5H monosubstituted ring, and an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.8.
Benzyl alcohol has a 5H ring and a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>O singlet near δ 4.65, not a 3H singlet at δ 2.27.
2-Methylphenol is ortho-substituted: four different aromatic H, not two 2H doublets.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows a strong IR band at 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> (none above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: There are two ethyl groups. One CH<sub>2</sub> is near δ 4.1 and one near δ 2.3. What is each bonded to?
w: 1740 cm−1 with no O–H is an ester. Two quartet/triplet pairs mean two ethyl groups. The CH2 at δ 4.12 is on the ester O (O–CH2CH3); the CH2 at δ 2.32 is on the carbonyl carbon (CH3CH2–C=O). The compound is ethyl propanoate.
x: Methyl butanoate would show a 3H OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near δ 3.67 and a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet; it has only one CH<sub>3</sub> triplet.
Propyl acetate would show a 3H acetyl singlet near δ 2.05 and an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet near δ 4.0.
Pentanoic acid would show a broad 3300–2500 cm<sup>−1</sup> O–H, a C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a δ 11–12 COOH signal.

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N shows a sharp, medium IR band at 2245 cm<sup>−1</sup>, a <sup>13</sup>C signal at δ 121.6, and the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure fits?
h: Identify the group from the 2245 cm<sup>−1</sup> band and the δ 121.6 carbon. Then use the splitting of the alkyl signals.
w: A sharp 2245 cm−1 band and a 13C signal near δ 120 mean a nitrile (DBE 6 = ring + C≡N). The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring. A 1H quartet (δ 3.89) and 3H doublet (δ 1.64) form a CH–CH3 unit; the CH is benzylic and next to C≡N. The compound is 2-phenylpropanenitrile.
x: 3-Phenylpropanenitrile has –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN: two 2H triplets near δ 2.95 and 2.6, no 3H doublet.
4-Ethylbenzonitrile is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets) with an ethyl quartet near δ 2.7 and triplet near δ 1.25; its aryl nitrile absorbs near 2228 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
2-(4-Methylphenyl)acetonitrile is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets) and shows two singlets (CH<sub>2</sub> near δ 3.7, CH<sub>3</sub> near δ 2.35).

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR and <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra shown (the δ 5.6 signal exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O). Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H bands with C=O near 1655 cm<sup>−1</sup>: which N-containing group? Then check the aromatic integration and what the CH<sub>2</sub> is between.
w: Two N–H stretches (3350, 3170 cm−1) with a low C=O (1655 cm−1) are a primary amide, CONH2 (2H broad at δ 5.6). The 5H multiplet is a monosubstituted ring, and the 2H singlet at δ 3.57 is a CH2 between the ring and C=O. The compound is 2-phenylacetamide.
x: N-Methylbenzamide is a secondary amide: one N–H band and an N–CH<sub>3</sub> doublet near δ 3.0 (coupled to N–H), with no CH<sub>2</sub>.
Acetanilide is a secondary amide (one N–H) with a 3H acetyl singlet near δ 2.15.
4-Aminoacetophenone also has two N–H bands and a low C=O, but it is para-disubstituted (two 2H doublets, 4 ArH) and has a 3H singlet near δ 2.5 instead of a 2H CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: Which <sup>1</sup>H NMR data (CDCl<sub>3</sub>) fit the product of the reaction shown?
h: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces an amide C=O all the way to CH<sub>2</sub>, keeping the C–N bond.
w: LiAlH4 reduces amides to amines: C(=O)NHCH3 becomes CH2NHCH3, giving N-methylbenzylamine. Its spectrum: 5H phenyl, a benzylic CH2N singlet near δ 3.75, an N–CH3 singlet near δ 2.45 and a small broad N–H: δ 7.30 (m, 5H), 3.75 (s, 2H), 2.45 (s, 3H), 1.4 (br s, 1H). The CH3 is a singlet because N–H coupling is usually not seen in amines (fast exchange).
x: These are the data of the starting amide (ortho ArH near δ 7.75 next to C=O, amide N–H near δ 6.2, N–CH<sub>3</sub> doublet near δ 3.0); LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does reduce amides.
Benzyl alcohol would require breaking the C–N bond. With LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, the oxygen leaves (as an aluminate) and the nitrogen stays.
Benzaldehyde (δ 9.99) is not the product: amide reduction by LiAlH<sub>4</sub> passes through an iminium ion that is reduced again, so it does not stop at an aldehyde.

q: A compound C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives the IR, <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra shown. Which structure fits?
h: Start with the carbonyl carbon in the 13C spectrum and the C=O stretch: which carbonyl class and is it conjugated? Then place the three singlets.
w: The 13C signal at δ 206.9 and the IR band at 1715 cm−1 fit an unconjugated ketone (an ester would be near 170, a conjugated ketone near 197 and 1680 cm−1). The 3H singlet at δ 2.14 (13C 29.1) is CH3C=O, the 2H singlet at δ 3.63 (13C 50.1) is ArCH2C=O, and the 3H singlet at δ 3.79 (13C 55.2) with the strong 1250 cm−1 band is an aryl OCH3. Two 2H doublets mean para. The compound is 1-(4-methoxyphenyl)propan-2-one.
x: 1-(4-Methoxyphenyl)propan-1-one is a conjugated ketone (C=O near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup>, 13C near δ 200) with an ethyl quartet/triplet, not two singlets.
Methyl 2-(4-methylphenyl)acetate has three similar singlets, but it is an ester: 13C C=O near δ 172, IR near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and no carbon near δ 207.
1-(4-Ethoxyphenyl)ethan-1-one has an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet near δ 4.1 and a triplet near δ 1.4, and its conjugated ketone has 13C near δ 197 and IR near 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
